title: Conjecture 7
statement_text: For any fixed integer $c \geq 2$, there exists an integer $t$ such that for infinitely many graphs $H$ with treewidth $t$ and paths $P$, every $c$-colouring of $H \boxtimes P$ has clustering $\Omega(|V(H \boxtimes P)|^{c/(c^2-c+1)})$.
context_text: A $c$-colouring assigns one of at most $c$ colours to each vertex, adjacent vertices being allowed the same colour. It has clustering $k$ if the largest monochromatic component (component of the subgraph induced by one colour class) has $k$ vertices. $H_1\boxtimes H_2$ is the strong product: vertex set $V(H_1)\times V(H_2)$, distinct $(u,v),(u',v')$ adjacent if $u=u'$ or $uu'\in E(H_1)$, and $v=v'$ or $vv'\in E(H_2)$. Products of a bounded-treewidth graph with a path are motivated by product structure theorems (e.g. planar graphs are subgraphs of such products), and graphs of treewidth $t$ are properly $(t+1)$-colourable, so only $c<(t+1)^2$ is interesting. With $n=|V(H_1\boxtimes H_2)|$, the authors prove the following. With 2 colours, clustering $\Theta(n^{2/3})$ is optimal, even when one factor is a path. With 3 colours and $H_2$ of bounded degree, $\Theta(n^{3/7})$ is optimal, with a lower-bound construction where $H_2$ is a path. For every $c$, if $H_1,H_2$ have treewidth at most $t$ and $H_2$ has maximum degree at most $\Delta$, then $H_1\boxtimes H_2$ is $c$-colourable with clustering $O(n^{c/(c^2-c+1)})$. Conversely, for $c\ge3$ there are graphs $H$ of treewidth $c$ and paths $P$ for which every $c$-colouring of $H\boxtimes P$ has clustering $\Omega(n^{1/(c-2/3)})$. The conjecture states that the upper bound is tight with the bounded-degree factor a path. It holds for $c=2$ ($c/(c^2-c+1)=2/3$) and $c=3$ ($3/7$) by the results above, so it is open for $c\ge4$.

title: Conjecture 8
statement_text: There exists a positive integer $t$ such that for infinitely many graphs $H_1, H_2$ with treewidth $t$, every $3$-colouring of $H_1 \boxtimes H_2$ has clustering $\Omega(|V(H_1 \boxtimes H_2)|^{4/7})$.
context_text: A $c$-colouring assigns one of at most $c$ colours to each vertex, adjacent vertices being allowed the same colour. It has clustering $k$ if the largest monochromatic component (component of the subgraph induced by one colour class) has $k$ vertices. $H_1\boxtimes H_2$ is the strong product: vertex set $V(H_1)\times V(H_2)$, distinct $(u,v),(u',v')$ adjacent if $u=u'$ or $uu'\in E(H_1)$, and $v=v'$ or $vv'\in E(H_2)$. Products of a bounded-treewidth graph with a path are motivated by product structure theorems (e.g. planar graphs are subgraphs of such products), and graphs of treewidth $t$ are properly $(t+1)$-colourable, so only $c<(t+1)^2$ is interesting. With $n=|V(H_1\boxtimes H_2)|$, the authors prove the following. With 2 colours, clustering $\Theta(n^{2/3})$ is optimal, even when one factor is a path. With 3 colours: if one factor has bounded degree, $\Theta(n^{3/7})$ is optimal. Without degree restriction, they prove that for any $H_1,H_2$ of treewidth at most $t$, $H_1\boxtimes H_2$ is 3-colourable with clustering $O(n^{4/7})$. The conjecture states that the exponent $4/7$ is tight, so dropping the degree restriction would genuinely increase the optimal clustering.

title: Conjecture 9
statement_text: For any fixed integer $c \geq 4$ there exists an integer $k$ such that for infinitely many graphs $H_1, H_2$ with treewidth $k$, every $c$-colouring of $H_1 \boxtimes H_2$ has clustering $\Omega(|V(H_1 \boxtimes H_2)|^{1/((1+o_c(1))\sqrt{c})})$.
context_text: Theorem 6 gives that $H_1 \boxtimes H_2$ is $c$-colourable with clustering $O(|V(H_1 \boxtimes H_2)|^{1/\lfloor\sqrt{c}\rfloor})$ when both graphs have bounded treewidth but no degree restriction.
